Marlborough 1848 · SW4 with explicit topography · prefilter arm · T ≥ 1 s

Which ridge should replace Brooklyn?

I checked each of your boss's candidates against the stations the run actually saved, scored each candidate against several flat reference sites instead of one, and drew every ratio over the spread that flat-against-flat comparisons produce. Sugarloaf is the only candidate that clears that spread. Otira holds up, but most of its 2.8× peak comes from the viaduct's valley shaking less.

Sugarloaf, Port Hills

The summit station is 410 m from the 121 m Kordia tower. Against 17 neutral rock references the ratio is about 1.0 at 1–2 s and rises to 1.6× at 3–5 s. Most references sit below the summit at 3 s, and the ratio clears the noise band. The rise with period fits the size of the hill: the crest features Kaiser et al. (2014) measured amplify at 1–3 Hz, and the whole Port Hills massif amplifies at 3–5 s. This is the scale argument your boss made, with Christchurch as the example. Recorded data from the Port Hills arrays can test it later.

Otira Viaduct

Measured against neutral sites, the ridge is 1.5–2.2× across 1–3 s, and the viaduct site is 0.52× at 2 s. The landslide framing survives, but the slide should say "slopes above the road shake 1.5–2× a flat site" rather than quote 2.8×. It also needs the period caveat in the red-team section below.

Brooklyn, Wellington

The 1.25× at 2 s sits inside the 10–90% range of flat-against-flat comparisons (0.74–1.29). Only 45 m of relief at the 1.25 km scale is too little for a model resolving 1 Hz and below, which is the scale point your boss made.

Ratio spectra

Each panel shows the pSA RotD50 ratio of a target site over its reference set. The line is the geometric mean over references and the coloured band covers the 16th–84th percentile across them. The grey band is the noise floor: the 10th–90th percentile of the same ratio computed at 5,870 flat sites against their own flat references. All panels share one log y scale.

Values at the periods the slide quotes

HD is site elevation minus the mean land elevation within a disk of diameter D, computed from the 50 m Copernicus DEM averaged to 100 m. A neutral reference has |H1250| ≤ 10 m, |H2500| ≤ 20 m and |H5000| ≤ 30 m: flat at every scale, not only at 1.25 km. References also satisfy |ΔVS30| ≤ 150 m/s (≤ 200 for Sugarloaf and WANS, whose VS30 is about 1000), sit outside the supergrid, and lie within 8 km (12 km at Otira, 10 km at Sugarloaf).

Otira: from the road up the slope

This transect runs through every station within 700 m of the line from the viaduct site to the paper's ridge site. Each station is scored against the same neutral references. At 2 s the ratio climbs steadily with elevation, from 0.52 at the road to 1.52 at the ridge. At 1 s the viaduct site itself is 1.48×, which matters for the structural argument below.

How the stations were picked

The Otira alternatives keep the two sites from the slide, the ridge fKtoMWL and the viaduct fKtnOWL. The only change is the reference: each is compared with every station inside the search circle that is flat at all three scales and within ±150 m/s in VS30. No reference was chosen by hand. I did widen the search radius at Otira by hand, from 8 km to 12 km, because only one station qualifies within 8 km. That rule leaves three references, 3–9 km away and in other valleys. The 32 orange squares are stations that look flat at 1.25 km but sit in a valley or on a slope at 2.5–5 km, which is the trap the slide's reference fell into. The ridge and the viaduct get slightly different reference sets because each one's VS30 window differs: the viaduct uses fNT4kWL, fZPVyWL and fZPSYWL. With three references, read the Otira numbers against flat sites as indicative.

The transect uses every station within 700 m of the straight line from the viaduct site to the ridge site, extended 1.5 km past each end. Each station is scored against the flat references within 12 km. The stations are the run's regular grid points, about 1 km apart here, not sites picked for the plot.

At Sugarloaf, the VS30 rule is what matters: it removes the 451 flat Christchurch basin sites (purple crosses), so the 17 references are rock sites on the flanks of the Port Hills and around Lyttelton Harbour. At Brooklyn and WANS, the same rules leave only two references and one reference respectively.

Red team: is Otira about landslides or the structure?

  1. Arguments for landslides. At 2 s the viaduct sits in a valley that shakes about half as much as a flat site, while the slopes above it shake 1.4–2× more. In this band the wavelength is 1–10 km against a viaduct about 440 m long, so the topography produces little differential motion between supports. The road's historical problem is slips and rockfall, and the viaduct itself was built to bypass the slip-prone Zig Zag section.
  2. The period band undercuts the landslide argument. Rockfall and shallow slides respond to short periods, PGA and Arias intensity. In this run, motion above 1 Hz comes from the stochastic HF method, which contains no topography. The simulation can therefore only speak to large, deep-seated failures. The Bray & Travasarou (2007) model uses Sa(1.5 Ts) with Ts = 4H/Vs, so a slide mass about 100 m thick in rock with Vs ≈ 400 m/s puts the governing period near 1.5 s, inside the band. Falling Mountain (1929 Arthur's Pass earthquake) is the local precedent. Say "large landslides", not "landslides".
  3. The structure is not cleared at 1 s. The viaduct site is 1.48× its neutral references at 1 s (three references, above the P90 of 1.26), and only drops to 0.52× at 2 s. If the viaduct's first mode is near 1 s, topography is not shielding it. Find the design period before claiming the structure is safe.
  4. "A 160 m ridge" undersells the relief. 160 m is H1250. The ridge station is at 1,838 m and the viaduct site at 881 m, so the ridge stands about 960 m above the viaduct, with H5000 = +530 m against −173 m. Quote the elevations, or H at the scale that matches the period.
  5. Absolute levels are small. PGA at the viaduct is 0.011 g and PGV 4.6 cm/s, so nothing fails in this scenario. Only the ratio carries over, and it would apply to a near-field event such as an Alpine Fault rupture. Present it that way, as a single sample from one event at 150 km.

Verdict: keep Otira and keep the landslide framing, scoped to large slides. Report the ridge against neutral sites (1.5–2.2×) instead of the ridge against the viaduct (2.8×), show the transect or say "the shaking roughly doubles from the road to the ridge", and add one line saying the viaduct is not shielded at 1 s.

Caveats

  • This is one event with explicit topography only. Without a flat-surface companion run, "topography at the structure" can only be approximated with neutral references. A flat (NT) run of the same rupture would give it exactly.
  • The Sugarloaf references sit on the flanks of the same volcanic massif, a few hundred metres lower. The Canterbury basin edge lies to the north; if it affects references on that side at 3–5 s, it would lower the ratio, not raise it.
  • Tower periods: a 121 m mast's first mode is probably shorter than 3 s. Present Sugarloaf as an example of how amplification depends on the size of the feature, and get the mast's period from Kordia before claiming structural relevance.
  • Across the whole domain, the median ratio is about 1.05–1.10 for ridges with H5000 > 50 m and about 0.90 for valleys with H5000 < −50 m. Single-site ratios scatter widely around those values.
